problem: It says the receiver must track the schedule "chip by chip". Chips belong to DSSS; an FHSS signal has hops, not chips. A student will carry the DSSS chip idea into FHSS and think FHSS also multiplies data by a chip code.
fix: In fast hopping several hops occur within one data bit, so the receiver must re-tune to the right frequency for every hop and combine several hops to recover one bit.

problem: The sentence "Only a few universities teach this topic in depth" is repeated word for word from the lead, and the application list (GPS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, military) is also repeated from the lead. Two nearly identical sentences in a short chapter waste the reader's attention.
fix: Delete "Only a few universities teach this topic in depth" from Section 1 (keep it once, in the lead) and keep only the new point here: CDMA-style sharing of one band by many users.

problem: The answer "about 11 times stronger" does not say what the interferer's power is measured over. The jamming margin only holds when the interferer's power falls inside the spread band the receiver despreads; a student may read it as 11 times the signal power at any single frequency.
fix: State the assumption: the interferer's power lies inside the spread band, so the receiver's processing gain of 11 (10.4 dB) suppresses it by that factor. Answer: the interferer must be about 11 times stronger in power, within the spread band, to break the link.

problem: The answer is too thin for 3 marks and only gives half the reason. Coherent addition explains why the wanted signal survives, but not why it can sit below the noise floor: the despreader also narrows the noise bandwidth by the processing gain.
fix: Answer: the receiver multiplies by the time-aligned code, so wanted chips add coherently and rebuild the bit, while noise and interference are spread over the wide band and only a small fraction of their power falls in the narrow data band; the resulting processing gain raises the signal-to-noise ratio by about Gₚ, so the received signal may be weaker than the noise in the wide band.

problem: "5G and Wi-Fi combine spreading ideas with OFDM and adaptive coding" is loose. Modern Wi-Fi (OFDM modes) and 5G NR are not spread-spectrum air interfaces; only the older DSSS mode of Wi-Fi spreads.
fix: Wi-Fi's older 802.11b mode used DSSS directly; newer Wi-Fi modes and 5G use OFDM with adaptive modulation and coding instead of spreading. 5G keeps frequency-hopping ideas mainly in frequency planning, not in the data waveform.
